scope: OSTEP CPU and scheduling batch against frozen Tycho pages; candidate questions, not claim-level completeness

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 10, sections 10.3-10.5
comparisons.observation: The page correctly says the carrier scheduler is not a backpressure mechanism. OSTEP cache-affinity and queue-topology discussion explains why more runnable tasks do not imply more capacity, but the page does not need to import OS scheduler detail.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 51-53; OSTEP ch.10 §10.3-10.5.
comparisons.conclusion: The page correctly treats carrier scheduling as a performance mechanism, not a capacity or backpressure contract; OSTEP ch.10 shows cache affinity and queue topology affect scheduling performance without creating capacity.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 7, sections 7.2 and 7.6
comparisons.observation: Tycho uses mean residence time and rejects substituting p99 into Little's Law. OSTEP response time is first-run latency, distinct from completion/turnaround; Tycho's boundary is admission-to-exit, so the metrics should not be conflated.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction; name first-response versus completion if OS scheduling is cited.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 99-126; OSTEP ch.7 §7.2 and §7.6.
comparisons.conclusion: Tycho uses mean admission-to-exit residence time and rejects substituting p99 into Little's Law. OSTEP distinguishes turnaround (completion) from response time (first run); the two are compatible only when the metric boundary is named.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 10, sections 10.2 and 10.4
comparisons.observation: Tycho discusses serial work, locks, hot keys and coherence. OSTEP adds a concrete single global run-queue lock as a scaling bottleneck and a topology alternative; the page does not currently use a scheduler queue as its example.
comparisons.proposed_action: Optional example only; no measured Tycho scenario exists.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 67-86; OSTEP ch.10 §10.4-10.5.
comparisons.conclusion: Tycho discusses serial work, locks and coherence but not a single global run-queue lock or queue-topology scaling limit. OSTEP ch.10 supplies a concrete mechanism the page could use as an example; absence is not an error.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 10, section 10.2
comparisons.observation: OSTEP list-delete race corroborates the page's claim that coherence and a concurrency-safe collection do not enforce a multi-step business invariant; a lock or atomic transaction still covers the full check-and-commit decision.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 51-55; OSTEP ch.10 §10.2.
comparisons.conclusion: The page requires an atomic transaction or state-owner protocol for a multi-step invariant. OSTEP ch.10's list race shows coherence does not enforce compound atomicity; locks cover only the critical section.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 13, sections 13.3-13.4
comparisons.observation: The memory page separates managed heap, native memory, stacks, mappings and RSS. OSTEP address space is a virtual layout, not a resident-set measurement; the two can be compared only with an explicit translation and residency boundary.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction; keep virtual size, reserved memory, RSS and live heap separate.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 49-53; OSTEP ch.13 §13.3-13.4.
comparisons.conclusion: Tycho keeps managed heap, native memory, stacks, mappings and RSS distinct. OSTEP address space is a virtual layout, not a resident-set measurement; the terms should not be mapped one-to-one.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 14, sections 14.1-14.5
comparisons.observation: The diagnostic page keeps GC pauses, RSS growth, native buffers and connection waits separate. OSTEP memory API focuses on allocation ownership, lifetime and invalid frees; those are different failure classes from managed retention and paging.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction; the page already avoids treating heap occupancy as diagnosis.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 71-82; OSTEP ch.14 §14.1-14.5.
comparisons.conclusion: Tycho separates GC pauses, RSS growth, native buffers and connection waits. OSTEP memory API focuses on allocation ownership, lifetime and invalid frees; these are different failure classes.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 13, section 13.4
comparisons.observation: Tycho describes a VM as a guest-OS/hypervisor isolation boundary. OSTEP process address-space protection is a narrower mechanism inside one OS; the two isolation claims should not be treated as interchangeable.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction; name the boundary whenever isolation is claimed.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 61-64; OSTEP ch.13 §13.4.
comparisons.conclusion: Tycho describes a VM as a guest-OS/hypervisor isolation boundary. OSTEP process address-space protection is a narrower mechanism inside one OS; the two isolation claims are not interchangeable.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 24, Summary Dialogue on Memory Virtualization
comparisons.observation: The latency page decomposes wall-clock time and lists GC, native memory, blocking and dependency waits. OSTEP adds TLB coverage and page-table walk cost as possible memory-stall causes; those are not visible in heap occupancy or GC pause data.
comparisons.proposed_action: Optional addition only when memory stalls do not fit heap or GC evidence.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 49-87; OSTEP ch.24.
comparisons.conclusion: Tycho's latency hypotheses include JVM/runtime/OS scheduling and native memory but not TLB coverage or page-table walk cost. OSTEP ch.24 adds that diagnostic hypothesis; absence is not a contradiction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 28, sections 28.1-28.14
comparisons.observation: Tycho says a JVM-local semaphore cannot serialize writes across replicas and requires a state-owner protocol. OSTEP lock mechanics corroborate the narrower claim that mutual exclusion covers one critical section, not a distributed business invariant.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 51-55; OSTEP ch.28 §28.1-28.2.
comparisons.conclusion: Tycho correctly limits a JVM-local lock to one process and requires distributed authority for cross-replica invariants. OSTEP ch.28 shows mutual exclusion covers one critical section only.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 33, sections 33.1-33.5
comparisons.observation: Tycho explains that publishOn/subscribeOn and boundedElastic move work but do not make a blocking driver asynchronous. OSTEP event-based concurrency shows the same boundary from the OS side: one event loop and nonblocking I/O, with blocking calls as the failure mode.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction; keep OS event loop and Reactor scheduler distinct.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 50-54; OSTEP ch.33 §33.1-33.5.
comparisons.conclusion: Tycho says scheduler choice does not make a synchronous driver nonblocking. OSTEP's event loop shows the same boundary from the OS side: one loop plus nonblocking I/O, with blocking calls as the failure mode.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 42, sections 42.1-42.4
comparisons.observation: Tycho asks what is durable when a primary acknowledges. OSTEP journaling makes the same point at the file-system layer: a transaction-end commit and ordered data-before-commit are protocol conditions, not properties implied by writing a log.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction; keep acknowledgment, log commit and data durability separate.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 51-60; OSTEP ch.42 §42.3.
comparisons.conclusion: Tycho asks what is durable at COMMIT acknowledgment. OSTEP journaling makes the same point at the file-system layer: TxE commit and ordered data-before-commit are protocol conditions, not implied by writing a log.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 48, sections 48.1-48.6
comparisons.observation: Tycho distinguishes replica and acknowledgment conditions for durability and availability. OSTEP reliable messaging shows why an acknowledgment can be lost after the effect and why duplicate delivery is a separate problem; exactly-once is conditional, not automatic.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction; keep acknowledgment, replication and effect identity separate.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 46-60; OSTEP ch.48 §48.2-48.5.
comparisons.conclusion: Tycho distinguishes replica and acknowledgment conditions. OSTEP reliable messaging explains lost acknowledgments and duplicate delivery; exactly-once is conditional, not automatic.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 53, sections 53.1-53.6
comparisons.observation: Tycho starts from protected outcomes and an explicit threat model. OSTEP connects that stance to OS-controlled resources and the cost of complete mediation; the two are compatible, and neither establishes a specific adversarial capability by itself.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 51-60; OSTEP ch.53 §53.2-53.4.
comparisons.conclusion: Tycho starts from protected assets, principals and trust boundaries. OSTEP ch.53 grounds the same stance in OS-controlled resources and complete mediation, without establishing a specific adversary capability.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 55, sections 55.1-55.6
comparisons.observation: Tycho separates identity, authorization and isolation. OSTEP access control shows the same separation at the reference-monitor level: authentication establishes a principal, authorization decides an access, and the enforcement mechanism has its own cost and revocation limits.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction; do not let authentication stand in for authorization.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 50-60; OSTEP ch.55 §55.1-55.3.
comparisons.conclusion: Tycho separates identity, authorization and isolation. OSTEP access control shows authentication establishes a principal while authorization decides a specific access; the enforcement mechanism has its own cost and revocation limits.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP appendix D, Monitors (Deprecated)
comparisons.observation: Tycho separates concurrency-safe data structures from business invariants. OSTEP monitors show that implicit locking still needs a predicate and wake-up discipline; automatic exclusion does not establish the invariant either.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction; keep predicate and wake-up protocol explicit.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 51-55; OSTEP appendix D §D.2-D.6.
comparisons.conclusion: Tycho separates concurrency-safe structures from business invariants. OSTEP monitors show automatic locking still needs a predicate and wake-up discipline; automatic exclusion does not establish the invariant either.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP appendix B, Virtual Machine Monitors
comparisons.observation: Tycho treats a VM as a guest-OS/hypervisor isolation boundary. OSTEP adds trap forwarding, double address translation and shadow TLBs as the mechanism behind that boundary; the deployment label alone does not prove the boundary holds.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction; name the hypervisor mechanism in isolation claims.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 61-64; OSTEP appendix B §B.3-B.5.
comparisons.conclusion: Tycho treats a VM as a guest-OS/hypervisor boundary. OSTEP adds trap forwarding, double address translation and shadow TLBs as the mechanism behind it; a deployment label does not prove the boundary holds.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Candidate comparison, not a claim-level audit of the whole page or source.

comparisons.source_unit: JEP 491, Synchronize Virtual Threads without Pinning
comparisons.observation: The page records that the canonical JEP 491 body was not fully accessible during the original research and keeps that limitation as historical provenance. R016 now reads the body: the revised bounded claim matches it, while the LM_LEGACY caveat remains implementation-review-only.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 132-136; JEP 491 Description, residual pinning and diagnostics sections (R016).
comparisons.conclusion: The page claim is consistent with the now-available JEP body. The remaining caveat is about implementation-specific LM_LEGACY behavior, not the JEP text.
comparisons.finding: candidate provenance update, no book edit under #225
comparisons.proposed_action: If the owner later edits the page, cite R016 and retire the inaccessible-body caveat while keeping the LM_LEGACY implementation-review limit.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; no implementation inspection or independent review.

comparisons.source_unit: JEP 444, Virtual Threads
comparisons.observation: The page correctly says interruption is a cancellation request, not a rollback. JEP 444 adds a concrete side effect for virtual threads: interrupting socket-blocking I/O closes the socket, so interruption is not a neutral stop for a connection.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 79-83; JEP 444 virtual-thread socket I/O and compatibility sections (R015).
comparisons.conclusion: The page is consistent but does not state the socket-closing side effect; the release boundary matters for JDK 21+ virtual threads.
comparisons.finding: candidate release-boundary addition, no book edit under #225
comparisons.proposed_action: If the owner later edits the page, name the socket-close side effect and the JDK/release boundary.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; no socket implementation inspection or execution.

comparisons.source_unit: Overload-control article, concurrency and CoDel sections
comparisons.observation: The page defines a precise queueing boundary and asks when averages can be related by Little's Law. R032 uses in-flight concurrency as an overload signal and reports that static quotas and fixed queue timeouts mis-shed; the two are consistent, but the article is first-party operations evidence.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 59-61; R032 sections Challenges and Building the Foundation.
comparisons.conclusion: The page boundary and the article's concurrency signal are compatible. The article does not supply a general proof that concurrency is always the right signal; it names low-QPS large-write and hot-key exceptions.
comparisons.proposed_action: No edit under #225. If the owner later adds an example, keep the workload and first-party status explicit.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; no benchmark or independent review.

comparisons.source_unit: CDC ingestion migration, shadow and reverse-shadow sections
comparisons.observation: The page lists shadow reads and CDC projection as mechanisms with failure conditions. R037 adds a concrete reverse-shadow phase, row-count/checksum equality, latency/resource gates and partition-level bad-data containment. The table is consistent but does not name reverse shadowing or checksum gates.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 51-60; R037 sections The Migration Lifecycle through Rollout and Rollback.
comparisons.conclusion: The page and source agree on the need for side-effect-free comparison and bounded CDC lag. The source adds a reversible reverse-shadow gate that the table could mention as an example.
comparisons.proposed_action: No edit under #225. If the owner later edits the table, consider reverse shadow and checksum gates as one example.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; no experiment or independent review.

comparisons.source_unit: Timeouts, retries, and backoff with jitter
comparisons.observation: The page says retries at two independent layers can saturate a shared pool even when each retry is below its local maximum, and requires bounded, capacity-aware retry ownership. R060 gives the same warning with the 3^5=243 amplification example and recommends retrying at one layer.
comparisons.basis: Tycho line 77; R060 Retries and backoff section.
comparisons.conclusion: The page is consistent with the source and already requires retry ownership, a cumulative budget and safe operation identities.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; no experiment or independent review.

comparisons.source_unit: Static stability using Availability Zones
comparisons.observation: The page defines control/data planes and says static stability retains pre-existing capacity and local state, while explicitly calling the AWS account a reported design approach rather than a universal orchestration guarantee. R061 supports that bounded claim.
comparisons.basis: Tycho line 54; R061 Static stability and patterns sections.
comparisons.conclusion: The page correctly keeps the source claim bounded and does not promise that every orchestrator has the same guarantees.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; no experiment or independent review.

comparisons.source_unit: The Tail at Scale
comparisons.observation: The page describes a hedged read as an extra equivalent read after an unexpectedly slow attempt, with an acceptable response and cancellation, and warns that it can double work when a shared dependency is saturated. R065 reports deferred hedges and tied requests with cancellation and bounded extra load.
comparisons.basis: Tycho line 83; R065 Within Request Short-Term Adaptations.
comparisons.conclusion: The page accurately states the mechanism and its key limits; the source supports both the tail-reduction claim and the shared-bottleneck caution.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; the reported benchmark is first-party and not re-executed.

comparisons.source_unit: Kafka Streams Architecture
comparisons.observation: The page compares Kafka Streams and Flink on state ownership, task migration, changelog restore and operational burden, and marks observed behavior as an evidence gap. R066 documents Kafka Streams local stores, changelog topics, log compaction, standby replicas and rack-aware assignment.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 51-59; R066 Local State Stores and Fault Tolerance.
comparisons.conclusion: The table matches the documented Kafka Streams mechanisms and correctly avoids claiming measured superiority. The source adds standby/rack details that are not in the table, but the table is not wrong.
comparisons.proposed_action: No edit under #225. If the owner later edits the table, consider naming changelog replay and standby state explicitly.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; documentation, not a recovery experiment.

comparisons.source_unit: Apache Kafka Design
comparisons.observation: The page keeps ISR status, acks=all and min.insync.replicas as separate conditions and warns that a smaller ISR does not preserve the same guarantee. R068 documents ISR commit, acks=0/1/all, min.insync.replicas and the no-loss guarantee only while an ISR replica is alive.
comparisons.basis: Tycho line 53; R068 Replication and Availability and Durability Guarantees.
comparisons.conclusion: The page is consistent with the design document and correctly bounds durability by live ISR membership.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; documentation, not a failure experiment.

comparisons.source_unit: pgvector README
comparisons.observation: The page says approximate indexes apply filters after the candidate scan, so a restrictive filter can return fewer rows and lower recall, and it names iterative scans, partitioning and partial indexes as mitigations. R069 documents the same post-scan behavior and mitigations.
comparisons.basis: Tycho line 52; R069 Filtering and Iterative Index Scans.
comparisons.conclusion: The page accurately states the recall boundary and does not confuse filtering with authorization.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; documentation, not a recall measurement.

comparisons.source_unit: OpenTelemetry Metrics Data Model
comparisons.observation: The page names sums, gauges, histograms and exponential histograms, attribute identity, timestamps and delta/cumulative temporality, and warns that the representations are not interchangeable without conditions. R070 defines those identities, point kinds, temporality and reset semantics.
comparisons.basis: Tycho line 79; R070 Metric Points, Temporality and Resets and Gaps.
comparisons.conclusion: The page accurately summarizes the data-model distinctions and does not treat the formats as equivalent.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; specification, not a backend implementation test.

comparisons.source_unit: RabbitMQ Reliability Guide
comparisons.observation: The page says at-least-once queue workers need durable progress and explicit dedup boundaries, and that acknowledging receipt can precede a durable application effect. R071 states that acknowledgements/confirms establish at-least-once, duplicates are possible after retry, and consumers must deduplicate or be idempotent.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 85-94; R071 Acknowledgements and Confirms and Data Safety on the Consumer Side.
comparisons.conclusion: The page correctly separates broker acknowledgement from the consumer durable effect and treats dedup as a correctness boundary.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; documentation, not a delivery experiment.

comparisons.source_unit: RFC 9700, Best Current Practice for OAuth 2.0 Security
comparisons.observation: The page says a token accepted by one resource should not automatically be reusable at another, and names sender constraints, audience restriction and refresh-token rotation. R072 recommends exactly those measures and explains cross-resource replay.
comparisons.basis: Tycho line 71; R072 Sections 4.9-4.10 and 4.14.
comparisons.conclusion: The page correctly separates token validity from audience and sender constraints and treats cross-resource reuse as a security failure.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; standards guidance, not an implementation test.

comparisons.source_unit: Statistical Analysis with Little's Law
comparisons.observation: The page treats Little's Law as an average identity for a defined boundary and warns against using it to predict tails. R073 shows that finite-interval averages are biased by edge effects and require a statistical estimator, not a direct equality.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 99-126; R073 Sections 2 and 5.
comparisons.conclusion: The page and source agree on the mean-only scope. The source adds the finite-interval edge-effect bias, which the page does not spell out; this is an enrichment, not a contradiction.
comparisons.proposed_action: No edit under #225. If the owner later expands the measurement boundary, add the start/end-empty condition and edge-effect caveat.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; paper not reanalyzed and data not rerun.

comparisons.source_unit: Making retries safe with idempotent APIs
comparisons.observation: The page requires a client request key scoped to principal/operation, bound to immutable parameters, with atomic token-and-effect storage and expiry tied to client retry horizon. R077 documents a caller-provided request identifier, ACID token-plus-effects, semantically equivalent responses, late arrivals and same-key/different-parameter rejection.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 135-153; R077 Reducing client complexity through Same client request ID.
comparisons.conclusion: The page matches the source contract and adds the client retry-horizon/expiry question. The source does not define a universal API contract, so the page correctly treats it as design evidence.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; first-party article, no execution.

comparisons.source_unit: PgBouncer Configuration
comparisons.observation: The page treats pool capacity as a fleet equation, distinguishes client leases from server connections, and warns that transaction pooling has session-state constraints. R078 defines pool_mode, default_pool_size, max_client_conn, query_wait_timeout and the session-state limits.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 67-80; R078 pool_mode, default_pool_size and dangerous timeouts.
comparisons.conclusion: The page is consistent with the configuration mechanisms and correctly refuses to equate configured pool size with database throughput.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; configuration docs, not a pool benchmark.

comparisons.source_unit: About Pool Sizing
comparisons.observation: The page treats pool capacity as a fleet equation and refuses to equate configured pool size with throughput. R079 argues for a small saturated pool, gives the (core*2)+spindles starting point, and explicitly calls sizing deployment-specific.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 67-80; R079 The Formula and Caveat Lector.
comparisons.conclusion: The page is consistent with the maintainer guidance and keeps the formula as a starting point, not a universal law.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; guidance, not a benchmark rerun.

comparisons.source_unit: RFC 9111 sections 3, 4 and 5
comparisons.observation: The page separates permission to reuse, freshness and authorization, and warns that origin failure does not grant permission to expose a response. R075 defines cacheable responses, freshness, validation and the Vary cache key.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 69-91; R075 sections 3-5.
comparisons.conclusion: The page matches the caching semantics and keeps authorization outside cache permission.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; standard, not a cache implementation.

comparisons.source_unit: RFC 9113 sections 5, 6.8 and 8
comparisons.observation: The page distinguishes connection, stream, attempt and operation identity, and says a GOAWAY last-stream boundary means streams above it were not processed while lower streams may have committed. R076 defines that boundary and request reliability.
comparisons.basis: Tycho line 71; R076 sections 6.8 and 8.
comparisons.conclusion: The page accurately states the GOAWAY boundary and does not treat a missing response as rollback.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; standard, no network execution.

comparisons.source_unit: PostgreSQL 18 chapter 28, sections 28.1-28.6
comparisons.observation: The page asks what is durable at commit and separates acknowledgment from data-page durability. PostgreSQL documents synchronous WAL flush, asynchronous commit loss window, checkpoints and redo from pg_control.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 51-60; R080 sections 28.3-28.5.
comparisons.conclusion: The page matches the documented synchronous/asynchronous distinction and does not claim that a WAL record alone flushes data pages.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; documentation, no crash experiment.

comparisons.source_unit: Jepsen read-your-writes and monotonic-reads definitions
comparisons.observation: The page states read-your-writes and monotonic-reads as session visibility properties and warns that neither implies global latest-state or a single write order. R087/R088 define the same properties but add the availability distinction: read-your-writes is sticky available, monotonic reads is totally available.
comparisons.basis: Tycho line 76; R087 and R088.
comparisons.conclusion: The page is accurate but does not state the availability difference between the two models; this is an enrichment, not a contradiction.
comparisons.proposed_action: No edit under #225. If the owner expands the page, add the sticky-vs-total availability distinction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; definitions, no execution.

comparisons.source_unit: What is a cell-based architecture?
comparisons.observation: The page says naming stateless workers a cell does not isolate a shared database, queue, cache or configuration publisher and asks which failures cross the boundary. R090 describes independent cells but also a shared cell router and control plane, and its 90%-unaffected example assumes even assignment and one-cell blast radius.
comparisons.basis: Tycho line 72; R090.
comparisons.conclusion: The page is consistent and stricter than the source: it names shared dependencies that the source treats only through the router/control plane.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; documentation, no failure experiment.

comparisons.source_unit: Multipart upload overview
comparisons.observation: The page separates logical upload identity, object key/version, multipart session, part position and expected digest, and warns that a completed multipart ETag is not necessarily MD5. R089 documents the initiation/part/completion lifecycle, part-number overwrite and the ETag caveat.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 71-73; R089.
comparisons.conclusion: The page matches the documented semantics and adds explicit transfer identities without overclaiming.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; documentation, no upload experiment.

comparisons.source_unit: PostgreSQL 17 explicit locking
comparisons.observation: The page names deterministic lock order, deadlock abortion and retry of the whole logical transaction. R091 documents table/row lock modes, deadlock detection, indefinite waits and advisory locks, including session-level advisory locks surviving rollback.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 69-77; R091.
comparisons.conclusion: The page matches the documented lock-order and deadlock guidance; it does not overclaim isolation from locks.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison; documentation, no concurrency experiment.

comparisons.source_unit: PostgreSQL 17 CREATE INDEX
comparisons.observation: The page treats online index work as a lock and deadlock concern. R092 states CONCURRENTLY still takes SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE, can leave an invalid index after failure, and that a failed unique index can continue enforcing uniqueness.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 69-73; R092.
comparisons.conclusion: The page is directionally correct but does not state the invalid-index and uniqueness-enforcement failure mode; that is an enrichment gap, not a contradiction.
comparisons.proposed_action: No edit under #225; owner may add the invalid-index caveat.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 33, Event-based Concurrency (Advanced), §33.2 and §33.5
comparisons.observation: The page claims that an event-loop server multiplexes many I/O operations across a small number of threads by returning promptly when an operation cannot complete, and that blocking the loop while waiting for JDBC, a mutex or an HTTP response prevents unrelated operations assigned to that loop from progressing. comparisons.proposed_action: No correction; optionally add OSTEP chapter 33 as an independent cross-reference for the event-loop blocking rule.
comparisons.basis: Tycho demand-blocking.md lines 50-52; OSTEP B083, chapter 33 §33.2 (threads-events.md line 43) and §33.5 (lines 187-189).
comparisons.conclusion: The blocking-consequence claim restates OSTEP's event-loop rule at the same conceptual scope; the WebFlux/Reactor and R2DBC examples are instances the chapter does not need to cover.
comparisons.finding: None; no factual conflict. The page's framework-specific details (small thread pool, reactive continuation, JDBC/mutex/HTTP waits) are not tested by this source.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Delegated extraction of one page section against one OS chapter; not a page-level audit, independent review, or runtime test. OSTEP §33.2/§33.5 models a single-threaded select()/poll() event loop, not WebFlux, Reactor, R2DBC, JDBC, or Netty, so the mapping is mechanism-level. Source read through a Jina markdown representation of the publisher PDF (version 1.10); raster figures were not inspected. The assigned range label R015-R080 did not resolve to OSTEP in readings.json; the actual full OSTEP records are B052-B116, and B083 is cited. Parent retains final classification.

comparisons.observation: The page states 'A thread is an execution mechanism, not a unit of business demand.' OSTEP introduces the thread as the abstraction for a single running process's point of execution: each thread has a private program counter, register set and stack while sharing the address space (threads-intro.md line 14). It justifies threads by parallel execution and by progress during I/O waits, and presents processes as the more suitable choice for 'logically separate tasks' with little data sharing (line 35).
comparisons.proposed_action: Retain the execution-mechanism definition; mark the 'not a unit of business demand' clause as an architectural judgment or add a scope note that OSTEP establishes only the execution/address-space distinction, not business ownership.

comparisons.conclusion: OSTEP supports the execution-unit half of the sentence and the process/thread separation, but it does not discuss business demand, task ownership, deadlines or cancellation, so the second half is an architectural claim outside the chapter's scope.
comparisons.finding: Partial support: the definitional claim is corroborated; the business-demand contrast has no source in this chapter and should not be presented as source-backed.
comparisons.assessment_limits: One sentence compared with one chapter; OSTEP is an operating-systems text and does not address service ownership, business operations, or Java task APIs. comparisons.source_unit: Lamport, 'Time, Clocks, and the Ordering of Events in a Distributed System', CACM 21(7), 1978 — The Partial Ordering, Logical Clocks, Ordering the Events Totally, state-machine discussion and Conclusion
comparisons.observation: The page says Lamport's happened-before relation distinguishes program order and message edges; that a Lamport-style counter preserves those causal constraints but does not prove two concurrent events are causally related merely because their counter values differ; that a total-order service or consensus is not clock synchronization and adds coordination, availability and latency costs; and that the paper defines the causal abstraction, not a running global clock or order service. It also treats a Lamport counter as insufficient for read-after-write visibility.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction under #225; if the owner later expands this passage, separate what R131 establishes (causal order, arbitrary total extension, participation cost) from client-visibility claims that R131 does not address.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 62-72 (especially 64, 70, 72); R131 'The Partial Ordering' (source lines 110-125), 'Logical Clocks' (166-200), 'Ordering the Events Totally' (201-226), state-machine discussion (289-334), Conclusion (448-471).
comparisons.conclusion: The causal claims are same-scope: R131 defines happened-before via same-process order, send/receive and transitivity and calls incomparable events concurrent (113-125); it states the Clock Condition as one-way and says the converse cannot be expected (176-185). R131 also calls the total order non-unique and dependent on the chosen clocks (209-226), and says the state-machine method requires every process to participate so one failure halts the system (316-323), supporting the coordination/availability cost. comparisons.observation: The page's section 4 frames a lost acknowledgment for an anti-corruption adapter: the legacy system commits but its response times out (line 68), so the adapter must repeat with the same scoped idempotency identity (line 71), query durable state by a stable business identity when only a status read exists (line 72), and must not treat blind retries as safe when neither mechanism exists (line 73). comparisons.source_unit: Ongaro and Ousterhout, 'In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm' (extended version, May 2014), section 8 'Client interaction'
comparisons.observation: The page's opening claim is that a client can lose the response after the server has committed, so 'no answer' does not mean 'no commit', and that repeating a state-changing operation without binding it to the same business intent can violate invariants. R132 section 8 records the same sequence in Raft: if the leader crashes after committing a log entry but before responding, the client retries with a new leader and the command is executed a second time; Raft's remedy is a unique serial number per client command, with the state machine retaining the latest processed serial number and its response and returning the cached response without re-executing a duplicate. The paper states the goal of linearizable, exactly-once execution between invocation and response and says these client-interaction issues apply to all consensus-based systems. It does not address HTTP method semantics, retention expiry, payload-conflict detection, or non-consensus transports.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction. If a mechanism citation is wanted for the chapter premise, R132 section 8 supplies the lost-acknowledgment/duplicate-execution sequence and the per-client serial-number remedy; do not extend it to HTTP or non-consensus transports.
comparisons.basis: Tycho line 63 (with lines 64-65); R132 section 8, source lines 765-779 (crash after commit, retry, unique serial numbers, cached response) and 812-819 (linearizable exactly-once goal and repeated execution), with the scope sentence at lines 803-804.
comparisons.conclusion: R132 confirms the page's lost-acknowledgment and duplicate-execution premise directly for a consensus-replicated state machine and states that the issue applies to all consensus-based systems; because the source is scoped to consensus systems and does not cover HTTP or arbitrary transports, the support is narrower than the page's generic 'in distributed systems' wording.
comparisons.finding: none; mechanism corroborated at the consensus-system boundary, no correction
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bound to one page and one record; R132 is a design/specification paper with no runtime experiment, and its two-column PDF extraction interleaves the cited passage across lines 765-779 and 812-819. This is not a full page audit or independent review; the parent retains final classification.

comparisons.source_unit: Chang et al., 'Bigtable: A Distributed Storage System for Structured Data' (OSDI 2006), section 2 'Data Model' and section 3 'API'
comparisons.observation: The page's section 4 claim is that an in-memory set fails across replicas and restarts, while a durable database uniqueness constraint or a state-machine conditional write can enforce one logical-effect record when scoped to the correct business domain, and its contract requires deciding duplicate status in one durable authority boundary and committing the business effect with the durable outcome atomically. R136 records that Bigtable makes every read or write under a single row key atomic regardless of the number of columns, and that it supports single-row transactions for atomic read-modify-write sequences under one row key while explicitly not supporting general transactions across row keys (batching writes across rows is only a client interface). The record therefore evidences a conditional-write primitive and atomic effect-plus-record commit only within one row; it does not evidence a uniqueness constraint, a cross-row deduplication table, consumer identities, or external-effect atomicity.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction under #225. If the page is later sourced, cite a store that actually exposes a unique constraint or state-machine conditional write, and state the single-key/row scope explicitly rather than implying cross-row uniqueness.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 52-58 and line 63; R136 notes for section 2 data model and section 3 API, source lines 95-100 (single-row atomicity) and 136-143 (single-row transactions, no general cross-row transactions).
comparisons.conclusion: The record supports the page's conditional-write branch only at a single-row authority boundary and explicitly excludes cross-row transactions, so it illustrates rather than establishes the page's broader 'durable database uniqueness constraint ... when scoped to the correct business domain' claim; it is silent on deduplication records and downstream independent commits.
comparisons.finding: none; single-row atomic read-modify-write is a narrower authority boundary than the page's general claim, and the uniqueness-constraint branch is not evidenced
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bound to one page and one record; Bigtable is not a relational store with unique constraints, the record reports no deduplication implementation or failure injection, and the two-column PDF extraction interleaves the API text. This is not a full page audit or independent review; the parent retains final classification.

comparisons.source_unit: Corbett et al., 'Spanner: Google's Globally-Distributed Database' (OSDI 2012), section 1 and section 4.2.2 'Read-Write Transactions'
comparisons.observation: The page's four-window trace says a consumer records a stable logical identity and changes authoritative business state in one local transaction, that the two writes belong to the same commit boundary, that separating them yields false suppression or double application, and that the boundary cannot include an independently committed email or remote API effect. R135 section 4.2.2 records a Spanner read-write transaction that buffers writes and then runs two-phase commit: the client picks a coordinator group, participant leaders acquire locks and log prepare records through Paxos, the coordinator leader assigns one commit timestamp, logs the commit record through Paxos, waits until TT.after(s), and all participants apply at the same timestamp; section 1 describes externally consistent distributed transactions whose commit timestamps are globally meaningful even though transactions may be distributed. This evidences atomic co-commit of records held in different Paxos groups inside one Spanner database, a distributed realization of the page's identity-plus-effect commit boundary, while the guarantee remains internal to Spanner and does not cover an external email or API call.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction. If a mechanism citation is added for the inbox page, cite R135 only for atomic multi-group commit inside one database via two-phase commit over Paxos and commit-wait; keep the external-effect boundary with the idempotent-consumer or delivery-provider source.
comparisons.basis: Tycho lines 62-68; R135 notes for section 4.2.2 and section 1, source lines 466-470 (two-phase commit begins, coordinator chosen), 476-486 (prepare records through Paxos), 488-511 (commit timestamp, commit record, TT.after(s), all participants apply at the same timestamp), and 53-61 (externally consistent distributed transactions).
comparisons.conclusion: R135 demonstrates that identity and business state can be committed atomically at one timestamp across multiple Paxos groups within a single Spanner database, which is the same commit-boundary property the page requires but at a different, distributed-database boundary; it confirms that the guarantee stops at Spanner's own data and therefore does not reach the page's independently committed external effects.
comparisons.finding: none; distributed-transaction realization of the page's commit boundary, external effects remain outside as the page states
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bound to one page and one record; Spanner's two-phase-commit/TrueTime design is not a generic inbox or consumer implementation, the record reports no inbox workload or crash-injection result, and the two-column PDF extraction interleaves the 2PC passage. This is not a full page audit or independent review; the parent retains final classification.

comparisons.source_unit: OSTEP chapter 29, Lock-based Concurrent Data Structures, §29.1 Concurrent Counters and the tip 'More concurrency isn't necessarily faster' (local representation /tmp/ostep/threads-locks-usage.md, 1,071 lines, 5,136 words)
comparisons.observation: Lines 88 and 195 report a benchmark where each thread performs one million updates to a single lock-protected counter on a four-CPU machine: one thread finishes in about 0.03 s, two threads take over 5 s, 'it only gets worse with more threads', and the text contrasts this with 'perfect scaling'. Lines 211 and 410-412 say per-CPU approximate counters scale because updates avoid contention, paid for by a global value lagging by at most the number of CPUs multiplied by threshold S. Lines 419-421 warn that added concurrency can lose to a simpler scheme and that both variants must be measured. Line 996 reports per-bucket locking making a hash table 'scale magnificently' while a single-lock list does not.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction; if this chapter is cited on the page, present it as measured counter/lock microbenchmark evidence for contention-limited scaling, not as a fitted Universal Scalability Law curve or parameter estimate.
comparisons.basis: Tycho scaling-models.md lines 82-87 (§3 curve shapes, fit caution at line 87); OSTEP ch.29 local representation lines 88, 195, 211, 410-412, 419-421, 996.
comparisons.conclusion: The page's qualitative claim that throughput shows diminishing returns under shared-resource contention and can fall when coordination work grows is corroborated in the same direction by a measured four-CPU counter benchmark. The chapter contains no scalability-model fit, no α/β interpretation and no service-level throughput data, so it supports the mechanism the page names, not the equation, its parameters or the diagnostics the page cautions about.
comparisons.finding: Candidate corroboration of the §3 curve-shape claim at a narrower boundary; no conflict detected in the read text.

comparisons.observation: The page states that ExecutorService.shutdownNow is best-effort and that code which does not cooperate with interruption may continue to execute (book lines 62-64). comparisons.source_unit: IEEE manuscript, 'Efficient and robust approximate nearest neighbor search using Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs', section 4 'Algorithm Description' (Algorithms 2 and 5; ef parameter), section 4.1 'Influence of the construction parameters', and section 4.2.1 'Search complexity' (local PDF extraction, 1,141 lines; cited lines 249-299, 333-345, 599-605, with the hub/degree passage at lines 155-166)
comparisons.observation: The page asks for explicit traversal bounds: maximum hops and returned results, edge type and direction, repeat-node policy, visited-state and request resources (L66-73). It warns that dense or cyclic graphs generate many possible paths and that a high-degree hub can make a path search expensive even when the graph holds few nodes (L55-60). R138 describes a graph search with several of these controls, but for approximate nearest-neighbor retrieval. The layer search returns at most ef neighbours (a result-cardinality bound), keeps a visited set that suppresses re-expanding an element within a layer, and terminates when the nearest remaining candidate is farther than the furthest current result rather than after a fixed number of distance computations (Algorithms 2 and 5, L249-299). Each element's connection list is capped at Mmax per layer (Mmax0 on the ground layer, L333-345). The paper's cost discussion makes the number of distance evaluations proportional to the degree of nodes on the greedy path, notes that greedy search tends to pass through the same hubs, and shows that a constant degree cap yields the stated scaling (L155-166, L599-605). The record does not discuss a separate depth limit, typed or directed edges, cycles, all-paths versus shortest-path output, or request-resource budgets, and its graph is a proximity graph, not an architectural dependency graph.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction under #225. If this record is cited, use R138 only for the narrower mechanism that result cardinality, visited-state and per-node degree can be bounded and that search can stop on a sufficiency condition; keep max-depth limits, edge type/direction, cycle handling, path-output semantics and the architecture-graph claims as page-local design guidance.

comparisons.source_unit: Search Engines: Information Retrieval in Practice (Croft, Metzler, Strohman), chapter 2 'Architecture of a Search Engine' (book pp. 13-29), section 2.3 'Breaking It Down', subsection 'Distribution' immediately before 2.3.6 'Evaluation' (printed p. 27, retrieved lines 573-581)
comparisons.observation: The page's owning claims are failure-mode claims: a cache can perform well under ordinary traffic and become a load amplifier during a key expiration, a write burst or an outage; expiring an entry and asking all waiting clients to refetch can overload a healthy authoritative store; and invalidating after a write can be undone by a slower in-flight read that fills an obsolete value (L62), with the chapter split stated at L64 and the decision to bound regeneration, hot-key fan-out and cold-start demand as part of cache recovery (L70-72). R219's only caching statement is in the Distribution subsection of its architecture chapter: a query broker distributes ranking across processors, and caching is described as another form of distribution in which indexes or ranked document lists from previous queries stay in local memory, with substantial time savings when the query or index term is popular (L573-581). That is a benefit condition for reuse under popularity; it describes no expiry, invalidation, concurrent refill, origin load or recovery, and no other record in the assigned batch was found to address cache-expiry load concentration.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction, and do not cite R219 as support for load amplification at expiry, stampede behaviour or invalidation races. The page's synthetic race and load examples are labelled invented and should stay labelled that way; source backing for these failure modes would require cache or queueing material that is not in this batch.
comparisons.basis: Tycho cache-invalidation-stampede-and-hot-keys.md lines 62-64 (load-amplification claims and chapter scope split) and lines 70-72 (bounded regeneration, hot-key fan-out and cold-start decision); R219 source lines L573-581 (query broker; caching of indexes or ranked lists for popular queries or terms).
comparisons.conclusion: R219 is silent on the page's claims. Its caching sentence establishes only that cached indexes or ranked lists pay off for popular queries or terms, which is the popularity premise a hot key presupposes, not evidence that expiry or cache loss concentrates load on the authoritative store; the amplification, regeneration, invalidation-race and cold-start claims are not addressed by this record or by the rest of the assigned batch as checked.
comparisons.finding: No support and no contradiction; the assigned record treats caching as reuse for popular work, not as a failure mode under expiry or loss.
comparisons.assessment_limits: One caching paragraph of a chapter recorded as fully read, compared with the page's integrated decision; the page carries no source_ids and its chapter ledger cites Redis cache-aside, Redis EXPIRE and Caffeine refresh, none of which was read here; absence of coverage in this record says nothing about those unread sources or about the page's correctness. Delegated evidence extraction, not independent review, human review, CI or source completeness; the parent retains final classification.

comparisons.source_unit: SRE Workbook chapter 16, 'Canarying Releases' (412 lines / 6,129 words; local representation /tmp/B20raw/sre/r163.txt), section 'Related Concepts' lines 346-379, 'Artificial Load Generation' lines 361-370 and 'Traffic Teeing' lines 373-379
comparisons.observation: Tycho warns that a benchmark can produce precise-looking numbers while measuring the wrong population, that a system which slows its load generator may appear more responsive, and that a synthetic workload whose key distribution, user decisions or failure mix does not resemble the stated engineering problem may yield impeccable charts and still choose an unsuitable architecture (line 64); it then makes arrival model, warm-up and outcome accounting the validity decision (lines 72-74). R163's 'Artificial Load Generation' subsection says load tests in QA, preproduction and even production are viable but caveated (line 364); synthetic load gives good code coverage but poor state coverage, is hard to simulate in mutable systems with caches, cookies or request affinity, may not model organic traffic shifts, and can miss regressions that occur only in events excluded from the artificial load (line 367). It adds that artificial load works poorly in mutable systems (line 370), and that traffic teeing through a shared cache can inflate hit rates and 'invalidate performance measurements' (line 379). R163 does not discuss open versus closed arrivals, a generator that slows with the system, coordinated omission, warm-up discard, unsent iterations, or demand denominators, and it treats load testing as viable with caveats rather than invalid.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction. R163 may be cross-referenced only for the synthetic-load representativeness and measurement-invalidation warning; the page's open/closed-arrival, warm-up and coordinated-omission mechanics remain outside this record and need the k6/HdrHistogram material the page already cites.
comparisons.basis: Tycho load-testing-and-benchmark-validity.md lines 64 and 72-74; SRE Workbook ch.16 (R163) lines 117, 364, 367, 370, 379.
comparisons.conclusion: The page's representativeness warning is corroborated at a narrower artificial-load/canary boundary, but R163 does not establish the closed-loop generator mechanism, arrival-model choice or warm-up/omission rules on which the page's validity protocol turns; support is narrower than the page's full claim.

comparisons.source_unit: SRE Workbook chapter 2, 'Implementing SLOs' (525 lines / 8,926 words; local representation /tmp/B20/raw/sre-workbook-02.md), section 'A Worked Example' lines 124-151, long-tail SLO rationale at line 138; percentile SLO table lines 234-235 and 243-244
comparisons.observation: Tycho says a system can have fast median service times and still miss a user-visible latency objective because waiting, parallel dependency calls, retry fan-out, queueing and uncertainty combine on the critical path (line 69); it says adequate mean capacity does not guarantee a tail objective when parallel dependencies and correlated delays can dominate the slowest path (line 79), and asks for end-to-end time allocation across critical paths, queues, fan-out and retries using distributions and explicit cancellation (line 77). R149 recommends multiple grades of SLOs 'to capture both the typical user experience and the long tail': if 90% of requests return within 100 ms but the remaining 10% take 10 seconds, 'many users will be unhappy', so a latency SLO should set multiple thresholds, 90% of requests faster than 100 ms and 99% faster than 400 ms (line 138); its worked example reports 90th-percentile 432 ms and 99th-percentile 891 ms and proposes 90% under 450 ms and 99% under 900 ms (lines 234-235, 243-244). R149 does not model parallel fan-out or correlated dependency delays, does not discuss hedging, retry amplification or cancellation budgets, and does not distinguish a measured percentile from the page's illustrative probability model.
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction. R149 may be cross-referenced only for the typical-versus-long-tail percentile rationale and multi-threshold SLO practice; fan-out amplification, correlated critical paths, deadline budgeting, hedging and retry-load effects remain outside this record.
comparisons.basis: Tycho tail-latency-fanout-and-deadline-budgets.md lines 69 and 77-79; SRE Workbook ch.2 (R149) lines 138, 234-235, 243-244.
comparisons.conclusion: The page's core warning that a good typical or median experience can coexist with an unacceptable user-visible tail is corroborated at SLO-design scope, but R149 does not establish fan-out amplification, correlated critical paths, deadlines, hedging or retry-load effects; support is narrower than the page's full claim.
comparisons.finding: Candidate qualified corroboration; no factual conflict or defect proposed.

comparisons.book_anchor: lines 67-69 and 103 (Purpose and mission; Integrated decision and reading route)
comparisons.source_unit: SRE Workbook chapter 7, 'Simplicity' — full-scoped text read, 342 lines / 3,385 words; cited passages L53-L55 (age as a complexity proxy), L123 and L134-L138 (Borg/Omega rewrite and migration costs), L150 (compare a rewrite with investing the same effort in the current system).
comparisons.observation: The page says modernization may legitimately end in 'retain and stabilize', 'upgrade in place' or 'modularize without distributing' (L67-L69), and later states that 'old technology is not itself evidence of a defect; retaining and improving the baseline must remain a real alternative' (L103). R154 makes the same retention argument for a rewrite: replacing a system wholesale may not be worthwhile because the new system must be built while the old one is maintained (L123); the Borg-to-Omega account adds a moving target, overly pessimistic estimates of improving the incumbent, and years of dual running during migration (L134-L138); and the lesson is to compare the expected rewrite result with what the current system would look like if the same effort were invested in improving it, while allowing that a rewrite can still be best (L150). Separately, R154 lists system age as one practical proxy for system complexity, citing Hyrum's Law and accumulated dependence on implementation detail (L53-L55).
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction. Keep the retain-and-improve alternative; if a citation is added, anchor it to R154 L150 (with L123 and L134-L138 for migration and dual-running cost). Add a boundary clause that age is at most an indirect complexity signal (L53-L55), not a defect, so 'old technology is not itself evidence' is not read as 'age carries no signal'.
comparisons.basis: Tycho legacy-baseline-and-modernization-evidence.md L67-L69 and L103; R154 r154.txt L53-L55, L123, L134-L138 and L150 (record status full-scoped-text-read, 342 lines / 3,385 words; the local file hash matches the record's representation_sha256).
comparisons.conclusion: R154 directly supports the page's central retention claim: a rewrite must be compared with investing the same effort in the current system, and migration and dual-running costs belong in that comparison. It does not support a blanket claim that age is evidentially inert, because it uses age as a complexity proxy; the retention argument is supported while the page's age sentence is narrower than the source's treatment.
comparisons.finding: partial support: the retain-and-improve alternative and migration/dual-running cost are supported; the age sentence needs a complexity-versus-defect boundary.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison of two page passages and one chapter; no modernization, rewrite or migration was executed, and R154's Borg/Omega account is a first-party experience report without measurement. The record's representation_gap field describes an earlier capture missing the byline, case-study headings and reader-action notes; the corrected file at the recorded hash (which I read) contains those elements, so the gap is treated as resolved for the cited passages, but the metadata inconsistency remains. Parent retains final classification.

comparisons.book_anchor: lines 82-86 (T3 authority-transition gate at line 83; failure test at line 86)
comparisons.source_unit: Ongaro and Ousterhout, 'In Search of an Understandable Consensus Algorithm (Extended Version)', May 2014 — full-scoped text read, 1,157 record splitlines / 15,150 words; cited passages L259-L272 (Figure 3 safety properties), L286-L310 (§5.1 single leader and stale-term rejection), L765-L779 and L800-L816 (§8 client interaction and duplicate suppression).
comparisons.observation: The page's transition table requires a '*fenced* single writer' at T3 and says 'never let two owners independently confirm' (L83); its failure test commits a booking, loses the response, retries while the canary is switching, and defines correctness as 'one logical booking and a discoverable outcome', not 'one HTTP request' (L86). R132 states Election Safety — at most one leader per term — and that a server rejects a request carrying a stale term (L259-L260, L286-L288, L304-L310). Its §8 client-interaction section describes the page's lost-response scenario: if the leader crashes after committing an entry but before responding, the client retries with a new leader and the command would execute twice; Raft's solution is a unique per-client serial number, with the state machine tracking the latest processed serial number and its response, so a duplicate returns the cached response without re-execution (L765-L779, L800-L816).
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction. If citing, use R132 §5.1 and §8 for single-authority enforcement (Election Safety plus stale-term rejection) and for serial-number duplicate suppression, and state the additional condition the page's canary scenario needs: the per-client serial number and cached response must survive the authority switch. Do not present Raft as evidence about migration, identity mapping, failback or fencing-token mechanics.
comparisons.basis: Tycho worked-adr.md L82-L86; R132 src.raft.txt L259-L272, L286-L310, L765-L779 and L800-L816 (record status full-scoped-text-read; local file hash matches the record's representation_sha256; the record's splitline map cites §8 at L800-L818).
comparisons.conclusion: R132 directly evidences the two mechanisms the page's gate depends on: one authoritative leader per term with stale leaders rejected, and duplicate suppression for a retried request whose response was lost. It does not address the migration/canary boundary, transfer of session state between old and new authorities, fencing tokens or a 'discoverable outcome', so support is at mechanism scope rather than transition scope.
comparisons.finding: mechanism support with a migration-boundary gap: single-writer enforcement and retry duplicate suppression are evidenced; cross-canary session-state transfer is not addressed.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison of one page passage and one paper; no consensus implementation, canary or booking system was run. R132 is a design/algorithm paper with a flattened two-column extraction (headings interleaved; figure images absent); the cited passages are prose and were read directly, while other sections were checked only through the record's section map and notes. Parent retains final classification.

comparisons.book_anchor: lines 85-100 (ranking caveat at line 85; fault rows at lines 95-96; proposed evaluation at line 100)
comparisons.source_unit: Introduction to Information Retrieval, chapter 8 'Evaluation in information retrieval' (pp. 151-175) — full-scoped text read, 1,342 record splitlines / 10,140 words; cited passages L50-L108 (§8.1-§8.2), L760-L862 (§8.5 relevance assessment, kappa), L1006-L1038 (§8.6.2 user utility), L1210-L1215 (§8.7 stale index/cache).
comparisons.observation: The page warns that a high-scoring retrieval result is not support for its recommendation (L85), lists 'high-ranking stale revision' and 'wrong but keyword-matching document' as faults requiring version checks or re-routing (L95-L96), and proposes an unexecuted evaluation over a versioned set of engineering questions with human source judgments, measuring support, unsafe claims and tokens per correct answer (L100). R204 states that relevance is assessed against the information need, not the query, and that a document is relevant because it addresses the need, not because it contains all query words (L67-L87), so keyword matching is explicitly not a relevance judgment. It also states that a document updated after crawling and indexing is reflected neither in the index nor in the cache, so neither accurately represents its current contents (L1210-L1215); it requires a judged test collection (L50-L66) with tuning on a separate development collection because tuning on the reported collection overstates performance (L98-L108); it measures user utility through task cost and productivity proxies rather than rank alone (L1006-L1038); and it reports that human relevance judgments are idiosyncratic, with only 'fair' inter-assessor agreement (kappa 0.67-0.8) even though relative system rankings stay stable (L805-L862).
comparisons.proposed_action: No correction. If a cross-reference is added, cite R204 §8.1-§8.2 for judged collections and relevance-against-need, §8.5 for assessor disagreement and kappa, §8.6.2 for cost/user-utility measures, and §8.7 for the stale index/cache hazard. Keep recommendation support, permission/authorization checks, unsafe-claim measurement and tokens-per-correct-answer as the page's own agent-route requirements, and note that a collection used for tuning should be separate from the one reported and that 'human source judgments' need an agreement check rather than being treated as objective ground truth.
comparisons.basis: Tycho question-routes-for-architecture-analysis.md L85-L100; R204 08eval.txt L50-L108, L760-L862, L1006-L1038 and L1210-L1215 (record status full-scoped-text-read; local file hash matches the record's representation_sha256; the record's section map agrees with these ranges).
comparisons.conclusion: R204 directly supports the page's retrieval-specific premises: keyword occurrence is not relevance to the need, a stale index or cache can misrepresent an updated document, and effectiveness should be judged on a judged collection with a held-out split and user-utility cost measures. It also cautions that human judgments are only fairly consistent, which bears on the page's 'human source judgments'. It does not address architecture-question routing, using retrieval rank as evidence for a recommendation, source permissions, safe refusal or unsafe-claim measurement, so the page's agent-route fault table and metrics are broader than the source.
comparisons.finding: partial support: keyword-match and stale-index hazards plus judged evaluation are supported at IR scope; recommendation-support, permission checks and agent-specific metrics are not addressed, and human-judgment reliability needs an explicit caveat.
comparisons.assessment_limits: Bounded comparison of one page section and one chapter; no retrieval system or routing experiment was run. R204's figure curves and two equations are degraded in the local extraction, §8.8 references were not the basis of any claim, and the page labels its evaluation as proposed and unexecuted, so no measured result is at issue. Parent retains final classification.
